title: My, your, his, her
description: Say whose something is in Brazilian Portuguese: meu, seu, nosso before the noun, and dele, dela after it.

guide.summary: A Portuguese possessive before the noun agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner: meu carro, minha casa. For his, her and their, Brazilians put dele, dela, deles or delas after the noun, and those follow the owner.

sections.title: My, your, our: agree with the thing owned
sections.text: Meu, seu and nosso change like adjectives, with the noun that follows them. A man and a woman both say minha casa, because casa is feminine.
steps: Find the noun after the gap: that is the thing owned.
Check its article: o or a tells you the gender.
Is it plural? Add -s to the possessive.
Pick the owner’s row: eu, você or nós.
watch: The owner’s gender never shows: Pedro says minha irmã, Ana says meu irmão.
Meu and minha look unrelated, so learn them as a pair.

sections.title: Several things owned
sections.text: When the noun is plural, the possessive takes -s too, and so do the verb and any adjective.
steps: Count the things owned, not the owners.
Several things: add -s to the possessive.
Keep the gender of the noun: meus for os, minhas for as.

examples.en: My keys are in the bag.

examples.pt: Os meus óculos estão na mesa.
examples.en: My glasses are on the table.

watch: Óculos is always plural: meus óculos, even for one pair.
Filhos and amigos are masculine plural even when the group is mixed.

sections.title: Our: nosso, nossa, nossos, nossas
sections.text: Nosso has all four endings, -o, -a, -os, -as, like an ordinary adjective. Many owners do not make it plural: only the things owned do.
steps: Look at the noun after the gap.
Pick -o or -a by its gender.
Add -s if there are several things.
watch: Nós moramos com nosso pai: several owners, one father, so nosso stays singular.

sections.title: Your: seu and sua for você
sections.text: In Brazil, você is the everyday word for you, and its possessive is seu, sua, seus, suas. They agree with the thing owned.
steps: Check that you are talking to você.
Match seu or sua to the noun’s gender.
Add -s for several things.
watch: Teu and tua, the forms for tu, are heard in some regions, such as the South. They are correct, but this course practises seu and sua.
For vocês, Brazilians usually say de vocês after the noun: a casa de vocês.

sections.title: His and her: dele and dela after the noun
sections.text: In Brazil sua casa would sound like your house, so his and her are said with de + ele and de + ela after the noun: o carro dele, a casa dela. These forms follow the owner, and the noun keeps its article.
steps: Put the article and the noun first: o carro.
Ask who owns it: one man, one woman, or several people.
Add dele, dela, deles or delas after the noun.

examples.pt: O irmão dele mora em Lisboa.

watch: Dele follows the owner, not the noun: the husband of a woman is o marido dela.
Never put dele before the noun: a irmã dele, not dele irmã.

sections.title: Their: deles and delas
sections.text: For several owners use deles, or delas when every owner is a woman. A mixed group, even one man and many women, takes deles.
steps: Count the owners: more than one means deles or delas.
All women? Delas. Otherwise deles.
The noun owned does not change this choice.

examples.pt: Ana e Maria visitam os pais delas.
examples.en: Ana and Maria visit their parents.

watch: O chefe delas: the boss is a man, but the owners are women, so delas.

sections.title: O meu or meu? Both are fine
sections.text: Before meu, seu or nosso, Brazilians may use the article or leave it out: meu carro and o meu carro mean the same. After a preposition the article usually stays and contracts: na minha casa.
steps: Before meu, seu, nosso: the article is optional.
With dele, dela, deles, delas: keep the article before the noun.
watch: Dele works differently: a casa dele needs its article.

steps: Find the noun owned and check its article.
Masculine takes meu, feminine takes minha.
Ignore the speaker’s gender.
Count the things owned.
Several: meus for masculine, minhas for feminine.
Make the verb and adjective plural too.
Look at the noun owned.
Pick nosso or nossa by its gender.
Add -s only if the things owned are several.
Talking to você? Use seu or sua.
Match the gender of the noun owned.
Add -s for several things.
Put the article and noun first.
One man owns it: dele. One woman: dela.
Do not use seu for his or her.
Several owners: deles or delas.
Only women: delas. Men or mixed: deles.
The noun owned does not decide it.
